attractions.name: Faisal Mosque
attractions.description: One of the largest mosques in the world, with striking modern triangular architecture at the foot of the Margalla Hills — Islamabad's most iconic landmark.

attractions.name: Pakistan Monument & Museum
attractions.description: A national monument shaped like a blooming flower, symbolizing Pakistan's four provinces and territories, with an adjoining museum on the country's history.

attractions.name: Lok Virsa Museum
attractions.description: A heritage museum showcasing Pakistan's folk culture, crafts, and traditions from across all provinces.

attractions.name: Blue Area & Red Zone
attractions.description: Islamabad's central business district and government zone, home to Parliament House, the Supreme Court, and major commercial towers.

food_places.name: Jinnah Super Market food street
food_places.specialty: A popular F-7 dining hub with a wide range of restaurants and cafes

food_places.name: Centaurus Mall food court
food_places.specialty: Modern food court in Islamabad's largest shopping mall

weather_info.climate_type: Humid subtropical climate with four distinct seasons

seasonal_notes.avg_condition: Mild and green, 15-25°C, one of the best times to visit
Warm to hot, 30-40°C, with monsoon rain in July-August
Cool, 5-18°C, occasional light rain, Margalla Hills sometimes get a dusting of snow

travel_tips.tip: Spring (March-April) and autumn offer the most pleasant weather for sightseeing in Islamabad.
Ride-hailing apps (Careem, InDrive) are the easiest way to get around; the Metro Bus is a cheap option between Islamabad and Rawalpindi.
Zone I is one of five planning zones in Islamabad Capital Territory — attractions here are grouped by zone rather than by separate towns.

history.founded: Islamabad's core urban and federal zone, developed from 1960 onward as the seat of government
history.city_history: Zone I is Islamabad's primary urban development zone, home to the Red Zone government complex, the Blue Area business district, and most of the city's original F-sector residential grid.
history.province_history: Islamabad was purpose-built starting in 1960 as Pakistan's new capital, replacing Karachi, and was inaugurated in 1967. Designed by Greek architect Constantinos Doxiadis on a grid of numbered sectors at the foot of the Margalla Hills, it is one of the few purpose-planned capital cities in South Asia.
